candidateRows: Gettier cases show that justified true belief is incomplete and that modern philosophy lacks an agreed definition of knowledge.
This establishes the epistemological problem on which Ben builds his broader claim that conventional skeptical demands cannot govern religious belief.
Ben recounts Plato's account of knowledge and Gettier's counterexamples to argue that justification, truth, and belief do not provide a settled definition.
Religious skepticism has the same closure-based logical form as general philosophical skepticism and cannot be insulated from its defects.
The claimed equivalence supplies the principal bridge from Ben's general epistemology discussion to his attempted defeat of religious skepticism.
Ben formulates a closure argument using opposing propositions, substitutes Christianity and Hinduism, and says both skeptical arguments share one classical form.
Requiring knowledge to be sensitively or personally acquired destroys closure, so rejecting that requirement dismantles the basis of religious skepticism.
This is the principal inferential mechanism offered for Ben's opening contention that philosophical and religious skepticism have been defeated.
Using a Matrix scenario and a parallel claim of divine disclosure, Ben argues that Nozick's sensitivity condition undermines closure and is therefore rejected.
The claim that one cannot know Christianity is true without sensing that every other religion is false makes the skeptical argument invalidate itself.
This applies Ben's closure and sensitivity analysis directly to religious exclusivity, making it central to his stated case against religious skepticism.
Ben identifies the inability to know all rival religions are false as the key skeptical premise, then argues its sensitivity requirement implodes closure.
A skeptical argument against biblical reliability based on inability to verify that Constantine destroyed no early editions likewise invalidates its own closure premise.
The Constantine example is offered as an independent application intended to generalize Ben's self-defeat objection beyond religious exclusivity.
Ben presents a Bible-reliability syllogism, says its second premise assumes empirical sensitivity, and concludes that this assumption undermines the first premise.
Demanding empirical elimination of every natural explanation for Easter makes the skeptical resurrection argument undermine the closure principle it uses.
The example directly concerns a major theistic claim and serves as Ben's culminating application of his proposed refutation of religious skepticism.
Ben lists natural explanations for the missing body, observes that the past cannot be exhaustively tested, and argues that requiring such testing defeats the argument.
Ben's opening supplied no evidence for God's existence, and defeating one version of religious skepticism would not itself provide such evidence.
The objection directly enforces the debate's evidential burden and challenges the relevance of virtually the whole affirmative opening to the stated motion.
Ben's opening claim that refuting religious skepticism strengthens the affirmative case for God's existence.
Matt says Ben discussed justified true belief and a possibly straw-manned religious skepticism but never presented evidence that any god exists.
The relevant question is whether belief in God is warranted by evidence, not whether either side's belief qualifies as knowledge.
This reframes the dispute around justified evidence-based belief and rejects the knowledge-centered standard that dominated the affirmative opening.
Ben's opening emphasis on defining knowledge and defeating skeptical arguments through problems involving knowledge and closure.
Matt distinguishes confidence-level knowledge from warranted belief and maintains that the debate asks whether evidence justifies belief that a god exists.
Good evidence can rationally justify a conclusion that is false when the evidence is incomplete and later information improves the explanatory model.
This separates evidential justification from truth, supplying Matt's operative standard for evaluating belief without demanding certainty or infallibility.
Matt uses the former geocentric interpretation of available observations to argue that evidence may justify belief despite incompleteness and eventual falsification.
Critiquing skepticism and problems of knowledge is irrelevant unless Ben identifies the actual evidence and good reasons supporting belief in God.
The demand returns directly to the motion's central burden by requiring affirmative evidence rather than an indirect attack on an inapplicable skeptical position.
Ben's extended attack on a version of skepticism that Matt says is not his position and does not establish evidence for God.
Matt asks Ben to state what evidence exists for God, explaining that he needs neither a knowledge claim nor certainty, only belief supported by good reasons.
A reliable explanatory methodology should fit the available facts while excluding comparably compatible rival explanations.
This establishes the principal criterion by which the skeptical side assesses whether purported evidence genuinely favors God over competing explanations.
Ben Fischer's opening treatment of skepticism and the justification of knowledge claims.
After asking for actual evidence of God, Matt explains that a useful method must fit the facts and discriminate among incompatible candidate explanations.
Tentative evidence-based belief should arise from observable facts, testable models, falsifiability, replication, and methods that minimize error.
The move supplies the skeptical side's positive epistemic standard, against which the proposed axiomatic case for God is subsequently evaluated.
Ben Fischer's critique of religious skepticism as unable to warrant knowledge.
Using the completed-puzzle analogy, Matt shifts from certainty to provisional confidence and identifies scientific model testing as the most reliable available approach.
Anecdotal and testimonial religious reports do not provide enough investigable evidence to establish an evidence-based argument for God's existence.
This directly addresses whether the available religious evidence is good enough to warrant belief in God and explains the con side's negative conclusion.
Ben Fischer's contention that religious skepticism fails as a route to justified conclusions.
Matt compares the case for God with a prosecutor's evidential threshold, acknowledges abundant testimony, and explains why his continuing search has not yielded a valid case.
Belief in God is not warranted by default; the believer must first provide a good argument and supporting evidence.
The move defines the debate's burden of justification and redirects the exchange from disproving God toward evaluating positive evidence for God.
Ben Fischer's claim that religious skepticism lacks good arguments showing that God does not exist.
At the start of dialogue, Matt rejects any presumption favoring theism, requires affirmative justification, and asks Ben to present the argument omitted from his opening.
Every conceivable world requires a beginningless-independent first cause whose self-directed causal agency implies a conscious divine will.
This is the pro side's principal positive case: an infinite causal past is declared impossible, and the required ultimate cause is identified with divine agency.
Ben presents the ever-pending-birthday domino scenario, infers that every possible world needs an initial cause, and argues that the ultimate cause must exercise conscious will.
The domino argument is a first-cause argument built on an unsupported infinite-past model, while known time and causality belong to this universe.
This challenges both the characterization and the crucial infinite-regress premise of Ben's principal argument, while exposing a possible consistency problem for an eternal God.
Ben Fischer's domino argument that an infinite causal past is impossible and requires God.
Matt treats the case as cosmological rather than ontological, questions talk of time before the universe, compares the reasoning with Zeno's paradox, and asks whether God is eternal.
God avoids the infinite temporal regress objection because divine thought exists in an eternal present rather than a chronological sequence.
The reply protects the proposed first cause from the same regress objection used against an eternal universe by denying that God undergoes successive temporal events.
Matt Dillahunty's objection that an eternal God may face the same infinite-past problem as the universe.
Ben distinguishes subdividing a finite interval from traversing an infinite past, concedes the problem for a temporally successive deity, and instead posits an eternal divine present.
Claims that God exists outside time and in every possible world remain unproved, and Ben has not supplied a formal premise-and-conclusion argument.
The move targets the evidential status of the pro case itself, arguing that its decisive modal and temporal claims have been asserted without demonstrable support.
Ben Fischer's appeal to an atemporal God existing necessarily across all possible worlds.
After clarifying Ben does not mean God began, Matt grants that Christians hold an atemporal conception but asks how either atemporality or necessary existence can be proved.
A first cause is an inescapable feature of every conceivable world and therefore functions as an axiom comparable to basic logical or mathematical identities.
This restates the core justification for axiomatic theism by claiming that no possible-world description can coherently eliminate an originating cause.
Matt Dillahunty's conclusion that Ben had supplied no formal premises and conclusion to evaluate.
Ben answers the demand for proof by asserting that even a Matrix-like world necessarily has a first cause and that requesting proof of such an axiom is misplaced.
Calling God axiomatic supplies neither an argument nor evidence, because assumptions are used precisely where demonstration is unavailable.
This is the con side's direct answer to axiomatic theism: if God must merely be assumed rather than demonstrated, the proposal concedes the absence of good evidence.
Ben Fischer's claim that a divine first cause is an inescapable axiom analogous to logical or mathematical foundations.
Matt explains that axioms are not proved, distinguishes them from reliable derived conclusions, and argues that treating God as an assumption cannot establish God's truth or evidential support.
The available epistemological models do not make God's existence axiomatic, and treating it as an axiom concedes the absence of evidence.
This directly contests whether an asserted epistemic foundation qualifies as good evidence for God, which is the central issue of the debate.
Ben's claim that foundationalism is the remaining viable epistemology and can ground God's existence axiomatically.
After Ben's extended trilemma discussion, Matt cites a hybrid epistemology and argues that evidence-backed propositions need not be adopted as axioms.
If God can act detectably in the material world, empirical evidence should be available and an axiomatic assumption is unnecessary.
The move converts the abstract epistemology dispute into a concrete evidential test concerning observable divine action.
Ben's reliance on an axiomatic demonstration instead of presenting observable evidence for God's existence or activity.
Matt asks whether Ben's God can act detectably; after Ben agrees, Matt argues that detectability should permit empirical verification.
Miracles can provide detectable evidence of God, although any reported sign or wonder can be forced into an infinite regress of proofs.
This is Ben's direct attempt to identify empirical divine evidence while integrating it into his core argument about terminating justification.
Matt's challenge to identify something God can do in the material world that people can empirically verify.
In response to the demand for detectable divine action, Ben names miracles but immediately argues that their proofs remain vulnerable to regress.
A claim that miracles occur is inadequate unless a particular miracle can be identified and reasonably attributed to a god.
The challenge establishes the evidential burden for Ben's proposed empirical example and demands an attributable instance rather than a category label.
Ben's proposal that miracles are detectable divine acts while emphasizing possible regress objections before identifying an example.
Matt objects that Ben is anticipating generic skeptical responses and asks him to name a miracle that can reasonably be attributed to God.
The resurrection of Jesus is a miracle supported strongly enough by historical substantiation to count as evidence for God.
This is a concrete affirmative evidential claim for a divine miracle, directly addressing the debate's demand for good evidence for God.
Matt's repeated request that Ben provide evidence for a specific miracle rather than discuss the beliefs of absent atheists.
After being pressed to supply an actual example, Ben offers Jesus's resurrection and appeals to its purported historical substantiation.
Calling the resurrection historically confirmed enough for oneself merely reports conviction and does not present the evidence needed to justify it.
The move directly tests and rejects the affirmative side's concrete miracle claim for failing to supply its purported historical support.
Ben's assertion that historical substantiation makes the evidence for Jesus's resurrection sufficiently strong.
Matt emphasizes that Ben has stated his conclusion about historical confirmation without giving the underlying evidence an unconvinced person could assess.
The trilemma concerns models of epistemology rather than God, so its alternatives do not themselves establish that good evidence for God exists.
This identifies the alleged category gap in Ben's principal case: selecting a theory of justification does not provide evidence for the debated entity.
Ben's contention that the unfavorable alternatives in the epistemological trilemma support his axiomatic case for God.
Matt acknowledges possible epistemological models but argues that, under any model, Ben must still present evidence specifically supporting God.
Axiomatic acceptance cannot establish God because incompatible gods or non-gods can be adopted in the same way, leaving no means to distinguish them evidentially.
The symmetry objection attacks the discriminatory power of Ben's method and explains why axiomatic declaration cannot substitute for good evidence.
Ben's claim that an axiomatic demonstration is the strongest reason he needs to offer for believing that God exists.
Matt argues that without presented evidence, the same axiomatic maneuver could validate Allah, Yahweh, Scientology, or a no-God proposition equally.
The burden remains on the person asserting God, while the atheist need only assess the offered evidence and is not required to prove God's nonexistence.
This prevents the affirmative case from shifting its unmet evidential burden onto the skeptic and clarifies the debate's proper argumentative obligations.
Ben's suggestion that the absence of a successful argument against his axiomatic demonstration supports belief in God.
Matt rejects the attempted burden shift, explains his evaluative role, and gives Ben a final opportunity to present actual evidence before audience questions.
The strongest evidence is an argument anchored in an axiomatic proposition, because merely coherent or empirical support otherwise generates further justificatory questions.
This is a concise restatement and elaboration of the affirmative side's core standard for what could constitute good evidence for God's existence.
Matt's objection that coherentism is an epistemology for processing evidence rather than evidence itself, and that Ben has conflated the two.
Ben argues that a conclusion derived from an anchoring axiom is well supported and says his epistemological survey was meant to establish that standard.
An adequate account of knowledge must preserve implication and the closure principle even if the Gettier problem shows that justified true belief is incomplete.
This move states the epistemological constraint underlying Fischer's case and explains why he rejects revisions that would undermine scientific, legal, and philosophical inference.
The objection that Gettier cases defeat Fischer's account of knowledge and its use in his argument.
Answering a viewer's Gettier objection, Fischer concedes that the prevailing definition of knowledge is incomplete but argues that any repair must retain closure and implication.
Near-death and other extraordinary experiences are better treated as fallible, culturally shaped interpretations than as independently verified evidence for gods.
The move applies Dillahunty's evidential standard to a commonly offered class of religious experiences and supplies natural and cultural reasons not to infer a deity.
The suggestion that reports of near-death experiences and encounters with gods should create doubt about skepticism.

Dillahunty explains that skepticism already includes doubt, then compares near-death reports with culturally evolving alien-abduction accounts to emphasize interpretive fallibility and absent verification.
Religious skepticism does not strongly disprove God, while axiomatic foundational evidence is stronger than infinitist or coherentist alternatives.
This is Fischer's concise restatement of his main thesis, directly contrasting his proposed axiomatic evidence with skepticism and rival epistemological structures.
The request that Fischer restate the opening case or strongest points in one or two sentences.
In response to a request for a compressed summary, Fischer identifies resistance to religious skepticism and the comparative strength of axiomatic evidence as his two principal claims.
Avoiding both creation from nothing and an infinite regress is best accomplished by positing a freely acting first cause that initiates all other causes.
The move supplies a substantive positive argument for a divine-like cause rather than merely defending Fischer's epistemological framework in the abstract.
The challenge that if God caused the universe, God also requires a cause and something must ultimately arise from nothing.
Fischer denies that anything comes from nothing and argues that a consciously free first cause can terminate the regress by initiating subsequent causal chains from itself.
The argument supports generic deism or classical monotheism rather than Christianity uniquely, while multiplying interacting divine agents is disfavored by parsimony.
This response defines exactly what Fischer believes his case establishes and invokes parsimony to limit the range of deity hypotheses compatible with it.
The objection that the same philosophical argument could equally support numerous named gods from incompatible traditions.
Fischer accepts that his reasoning does not uniquely establish the Christian God, says it reaches basic theism, and argues that multiple interacting gods add unnecessary entities.
Testimonial miracle reports can count as evidence when reasonably credible, because excluding them through an overly restrictive sensitivity condition would also damage ordinary inferential evidence.
The move identifies miracle testimony as an offered evidential category for God and connects its admissibility to Fischer's broader defense of epistemic closure.
The challenge that a universe-creating God could easily settle the dispute by making divine existence plainly evident.

Fischer answers that miracle testimony is available and argues that a standard excluding such reports through sensitivity requirements would imperil legal, scientific, and philosophical evidence as well.
Epistemological systems help evaluate evidence but are independent of the evidence itself, and merely declaring God axiomatic is not thereby an argument or evidence.
This move isolates Dillahunty's core objection that choosing a justificatory framework cannot substitute for presenting evidence that actually supports the existence of God.
Fischer's claim that his demonstration qualifies as evidence because it coheres with axiomatic foundationalism.
Dillahunty notes alternatives to the traditional trilemma, questions whether axiomatic theism counts as evidence within those systems, and separates evidential content from methods of assessment.
A god relevant to human knowledge must manifest detectably, making its existence an empirical question that requires a demonstrated connection between observations and divine causation.
This is Dillahunty's clearest statement of the evidential burden: an undetectable god is epistemically indistinguishable from no god, while a detectable god requires causal evidence.
Fischer's continued reliance on epistemological trilemmas and axiomatic foundations instead of an observable evidential connection to God.
Dillahunty argues that an unmanifested deity cannot be distinguished from nonexistence, whereas any manifested deity becomes empirically assessable through evidence linking an observation to God.
If the presentation that God is axiomatically present in every conceivable world cannot be refuted, God's existence follows from being conceptually ineliminable.
The response states the decisive inference of Fischer's principal case, treating God's alleged conceptual ineliminability as sufficient for necessary existence.
The parody objection that one can prove the nonexistence of gods simply by taking their nonexistence as an axiom.
Against a contrary axiom asserting that gods do not exist, Fischer places the burden on critics to identify an error in his claimed demonstration of God's presence in every conceivable world.
Competing beliefs should be tested under shared and consistently applied evidential standards, which would expose special pleading in treating God as an assumed axiom.
The move offers an operational comparison for deciding which worldview handles evidence more consistently and directly challenges the special exemption granted to a God claim.
The claim that evidential standards must be shared and independently verifiable, alongside Fischer's treatment of God as axiomatic.
Dillahunty proposes comparing agreed and disputed beliefs, their evidence, and their evaluation across worldviews, then argues that consistent standards and parsimony count against axiomatic theism.
Theism remains rationally compelling because Fischer has found no successful argument for either propositional or psychological atheism.
The answer directly addresses whether Fischer's belief is defeasible and identifies the alleged failure of atheistic objections as a principal basis for retaining theism.
The question asks what evidence or argument could convince Fischer that God does not or probably does not exist.
Fischer recounts subjecting his faith to an existential and rational test, then says the arguments remain too strong and atheistic alternatives lack adequate support.
Fischer improperly shifts the burden of proof by treating the failure to defeat God as grounds for belief rather than requiring positive evidence.
This identifies the central evidential dispute: belief should follow positive supporting evidence, not merely the absence of a successful defeater for an opposing claim.
Fischer's account treats his inability to find a successful defeater for theism as a rational basis for maintaining belief.
Dillahunty characterizes Fischer's method as burden shifting and concludes that the proper time to believe is after evidence appears, not after objections fail.
A capital-C first cause resolves the regress of causes, and self-evident propositions can constitute evidence without independent verification.
The move supplies Fischer's principal positive rationale for God while defending the disputed claim that axiomatic self-evidence can qualify as evidence.
The question argues that assuming God changes nothing, unlike a geometrical axiom, and therefore fails as evidential support.
Fischer invokes an ultimate cause to halt regress, rejects the requirement that evidence be independent of its object, and endorses axiomatic belief as the strongest option.
Confidence should be proportional to evidence, and calling God axiomatic cannot substitute for demonstrating that God exists.
This directly articulates the skeptical standard governing the motion and applies it against Fischer's attempt to classify God as self-evident.
The question and Fischer's preceding position concern whether axiomatic belief can be warranted without proportionate empirical support.
Dillahunty invokes proportional confidence, falsification, and practical demonstration, arguing that mathematical examples can be shown while God has not been demonstrated.
Logical and mathematical axioms can be necessarily true without any empirical or operational instance demonstrating them.
The move defends the epistemic mechanism on which Fischer's axiomatic case depends by denying that fundamental truths require empirical instantiation.
Dillahunty argues that purported axioms need practical demonstration and uses observable arithmetic examples to support that requirement.
Fischer answers that laws of logic and mathematical axioms need no operational example anywhere in the universe to be true, marking a basic disagreement between them.
An experienced persistence of God's presence during doubt provided powerful personal confirmation of theism after philosophical objections seemed defeated.
This offers an experiential source of affirmative support for God beyond the abstract axiomatic argument and explains why Fischer retained his faith.
Fischer says that after finding no good philosophical reason for doubt, the continuing presence of the Holy Spirit during his worst trial strongly confirmed his belief.
Consciousness is not merely assumed but inferred from observable interaction and behavior characteristic of demonstrably thinking agents.
The response supplies a contrast case showing how an apparently foundational proposition can receive observable support rather than being declared axiomatic.
The question suggests that cosmological arguments illicitly assume consciousness and asks why that assumption is taken seriously.
Dillahunty defines consciousness through the capacities and interactions of thinking agents, treating their conversation as evidence and denying that consciousness is simply presumed.
The certainty expressed by the cogito is axiomatically true because denying it would also undermine knowledge that one occupies a world where it fails.
The cogito functions as a supporting example for Fischer's broader claim that some propositions warrant acceptance through axiomatic necessity.
Fischer supplements the discussion of consciousness with the cogito and argues that even imagining a universe where it fails would leave us unable to know we inhabit it.
An ultimate cause must contain conscious will because the reason it initiates all derivative causes must lie within the ultimate cause itself.
This is a concise statement of Fischer's positive inference from an ultimate explanatory cause to a conscious, purposive foundation identified with God.
The question challenges Fischer to provide his best reason for treating God as a sound foundation or as any foundation at all.
Fischer argues that regress terminates in a capital-C cause and that an internally grounded reason for initiating other causes implies a conscious will.
Axioms differ from presuppositions because axioms are self-evident irreducible truths, whereas presuppositions are merely assumed without self-authentication.
The distinction is essential to Fischer's defense against the charge that God has only been assumed, because it specifies the claimed evidential status of an axiom.
The question challenges how a controversial and nonconsensual claim that God is self-evident can become axiomatic evidence.
Fischer distinguishes two forms of foundationalism, defining presuppositions as assumptions and axioms as self-evident primes that rational inquiry is not justified in questioning.
Mathematical truths can be established through theoretical entities without requiring observable physical instances.
The claim directly supports Ben's broader analogy between axiomatic theism and mathematical knowledge that does not depend on empirical observation.
The questioner's objection that an unobservable God cannot qualify as an axiom because assuming God changes no observable result.
During audience questions, Ben defends non-empirical knowledge by arguing that mathematics may be known wholly through theoretical entities without physical operational examples.
Alleged biblical inaccuracies must be assessed individually, and the scriptures he has studied appear broadly accurate.
The answer protects the credibility of the Christian framework underlying Ben's theistic position against an evidential objection concerning scripture.
The audience challenge asking how a Christian conception of God can be defended given alleged inaccuracies in the Bible.
Ben declines to concede a general charge of biblical inaccuracy, insisting on case-by-case examination and asking what evidence supports each claimed error.
The sequence of events in Genesis 1 conflicts with the sequence indicated by scientific findings.
It supplies a concrete empirical challenge to Ben's general claim that scripture appears accurate and therefore tests his evidential standard.
Ben's claim that his study provides little ground for treating purported biblical inaccuracies as genuine inaccuracies.
After Ben requests specific evidence of inaccuracy, Matt offers Genesis 1's ordering of events as a direct example that conflicts with science.
Existing theological interpretations can reconcile Genesis with scientific chronology, though a full defense exceeds the debate's prepared scope.
The reply resists Matt's concrete scriptural counterexample by asserting that coherent reconciliations exist, preserving the broader Christian evidential framework.
Matt's assertion that Genesis 1 presents an order of events inconsistent with the findings of science.
Ben points to theologians, including Hugh Ross, who offer harmonizing readings, while acknowledging that developing those accounts would require a deeper discussion.
Axiomatic assertion is neither evidence nor an argument for God, while private revelation remains hearsay to everyone except its recipient.
The move directly rejects the debate's proposed axiomatic basis for theism and contrasts public demonstration with conviction and first-person revelation.
Ben's broader position that God's existence can be treated as axiomatically grounded and that this supplies an adequate epistemic foundation.
Answering what argument persuaded him as a believer, Matt says his faith relied on scripture and conviction, then generalizes that axioms and revelation provide no public evidence.
Biblical commands describing total destruction are ancient Near Eastern hyperbole rather than literal instructions to murder every member of a people.
The interpretation answers a moral-evidential challenge to the Christian God by denying that the relevant texts literally endorse indiscriminate slaughter.
Matt's challenge that commands to slaughter males and non-virgin women while retaining virgin women amount to instructions for murder.
Ben argues that commands to kill everyone conflict with commands to drive people out, and compares them with Jesus's plainly nonliteral instruction to pluck out an eye.
Calling conquest accounts hyperbole is not established by Christian noncompliance, and the textual narratives still require evidential justification for that reading.
The move contests the interpretive mechanism Ben uses to neutralize morally troubling biblical commands and demands a basis beyond merely labeling them hyperbolic.
Ben's argument that contradictory-sounding commands and figurative teachings show the conquest language should be read as hyperbole.
Matt presses Ben on how the historical conquest narrative becomes hyperbole, distinguishes textual commands from actual military targeting, and challenges the unsupported classification.
A woodenly literal reading cannot coherently require both killing an entire population and driving that same population out of the land.
This is Ben's concise defense of the hyperbole interpretation against Matt's demand for a reason not to read the destruction commands literally.
Matt's repeated challenge that Ben has merely asserted hyperbole without adequately establishing that the commands were nonliteral.
Before the moderator moves on, Ben reiterates that literal fulfillment creates an incompatibility between exterminating a people and expelling them from the land.
The permission to own and beat people in Exodus 21 creates a further problem that cannot be dismissed merely by labeling difficult passages hyperbole.
The example broadens the moral-evidential challenge beyond conquest language to a legal passage whose content is less plausibly explained as battlefield hyperbole.
Ben's use of figurative or hyperbolic interpretation to reconcile morally troubling biblical commands with the Christian conception of God.
As the moderator ends the exchange, Matt introduces biblical slave ownership and permitted beatings as a distinct test of Ben's proposed hyperbole defense.
A resurrection is more plausibly hyperbolic than commands to kill people or permission to own slaves, so selective literalism amounts to cherry-picking.
The move attacks the consistency of accepting the resurrection as literal evidence while treating morally damaging biblical material as figurative or hyperbolic.
Ben's defense of Christianity through a hyperbolic reading of biblical destruction commands while retaining other supernatural claims as literal.
In a closing aside, Matt proposes debating how hyperbole is identified and contrasts the resurrection with commands concerning killing and slavery to allege selective interpretation.
